pathophysiology.summary: ACS is myocardial ischaemia from an acute reduction in coronary flow, usually after atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with thrombosis. It includes acute myocardial infarction (troponin rise with ischaemia) and unstable angina. Complete occlusion (STEMI or other 'acute coronary occlusion MI', ACOMI) needs emergency reperfusion.
keyMechanisms: Plaque rupture/erosion exposes thrombogenic material → platelet aggregation and thrombus; partial occlusion gives NSTE-ACS, complete occlusion gives STEMI/ACOMI.
ACOMI includes ECG patterns beyond ST elevation: high lateral, posterior and right ventricular MI, De Winter T waves, and LBBB meeting modified Sgarbossa criteria (Australian 2025).
Myocardial necrosis releases troponin; high-sensitivity assays allow rule-in/rule-out within 1–2 h using assay-specific thresholds and deltas.
Complications: arrhythmia (VF/VT), heart failure, cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications.

symptoms: Central chest pain or pressure, may radiate to arm, jaw or back; at rest or prolonged.
Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, syncope.
Atypical presentations are common in older people, women and people with diabetes.
physicalSigns: Often normal examination.

redFlags: ST elevation or ACOMI equivalent on ECG → emergency reperfusion
Ongoing pain, haemodynamic or electrical instability, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock (very high risk NSTE-ACS → invasive within 2 h)
Cardiac arrest — do not use level of consciousness to decide eligibility for angiography (NICE)
precipitants: Atherosclerotic risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, family history.
Non-atherosclerotic causes such as spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD).

Pleuritic pain, hypoxaemia, risk factors; CTPA.

clinicalManagement.title: First 10 minutes
actions: ECG within 10 min; continuous monitoring and defibrillator if ongoing symptoms or ischaemic ECG.
Aspirin 300 mg orally (chewed or dissolved) unless contraindicated.
Oxygen only if SpO2 below 90%; keep SpO2 at 96% or lower if oxygen is given.
IV fentanyl or morphine boluses for chest pain if no contraindication.
Exclude aortic dissection when suspected before antithrombotics.

clinicalManagement.title: STEMI / ACOMI — reperfusion
actions: Primary PCI preferred if deliverable within 120 min of first medical contact (NICE: within 120 min of when fibrinolysis could have been given). PCI-capable centre: within 60 min of arrival; transfer: within 90 min of first hospital arrival.
Otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 min of first medical contact, with an antithrombin (UFH or enoxaparin). Age 70 or over: half-dose tenecteplase as part of a pharmaco-invasive strategy.
After fibrinolysis: ECG at 60–90 min — residual ST elevation → immediate angiography (do not repeat lysis); successful lysis → transfer to PCI centre, angiography within 2–24 h.
Primary PCI: DAPT with aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel (clopidogrel if these are contraindicated or on oral anticoagulation); UFH (or bivalirudin). No routine GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor.
Shock within 12 h → angiography ± PCI; no routine IABP or VA-ECMO.

clinicalManagement.title: NSTE-ACS
actions: Anticoagulate: UFH, enoxaparin or fondaparinux (NICE: fondaparinux if no high bleeding risk and not going for immediate angiography; UFH if creatinine above 265 µmol/L).
Very high risk (instability, ongoing pain, shock, heart failure, arrhythmia): immediate invasive strategy within 2 h.
High risk: early invasive within 24 h (Australian); NICE: consider angiography within 72 h if GRACE 6-month mortality above 3.0%.
DAPT: aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel if routine invasive (prasugrel only once anatomy known and PCI intended); selective invasive: ticagrelor or clopidogrel.
Lower risk: ischaemia testing guides need for angiography.

clinicalManagement.title: In-hospital and discharge
actions: DAPT 6–12 months (high ischaemic/low bleeding risk); then long-term P2Y12 inhibitor over aspirin (Australian).
On oral anticoagulation: OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel for 1–4 weeks, then stop aspirin (PPI with triple therapy).
High-intensity lipid lowering: LDL-C below 1.4 mmol/L and at least 50% reduction; beta-blocker if LV impairment; cardiac rehabilitation; vaccinations.

pathophysiology.summary: Ischaemic heart disease (coronary artery disease) is myocardial ischaemia from atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries. Stable angina is predictable chest discomfort on exertion or emotion, relieved by rest or a nitrate within minutes, caused by a fixed stenosis limiting flow when oxygen demand rises.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque narrows the lumen; flow reserve is adequate at rest but insufficient when demand rises (heart rate, BP, contractility) → supply–demand mismatch → angina.
Beta-blockers lower heart rate and contractility; calcium-channel blockers dilate coronaries and reduce afterload; nitrates reduce preload — all reduce demand or improve supply.
Plaque rupture or erosion turns stable disease into an acute coronary syndrome — secondary prevention (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and risk-factor control) reduces events.
Significant CAD on CT: 70% or more stenosis in a major epicardial segment or 50% or more in the left main (NICE CG95).

symptoms: Constricting chest, neck, shoulder, jaw or arm discomfort, precipitated by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes (typical angina: all three features).
Exertional breathlessness (angina equivalent), especially in older people, women and people with diabetes.
physicalSigns: Often normal examination.
Signs of risk factors or complications: hypertension, xanthelasma, carotid bruits, signs of heart failure, aortic stenosis murmur (alternative cause of angina).
redFlags: Pain at rest, increasing frequency/severity or pain lasting over 15 minutes — possible ACS: call ambulance
Pain persisting 5 minutes after a second GTN dose — emergency (NICE)
Syncope or breathlessness on exertion with ejection systolic murmur (aortic stenosis)
Symptoms uncontrolled on two anti-anginal drugs — consider revascularisation

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnose
actions: Assess pain typicality; ECG; CT coronary angiography first line when angina cannot be excluded clinically (CG95).
Treat as stable angina while awaiting tests if symptoms are typical; consider aspirin until diagnosis (CG95).

clinicalManagement.title: Relieve episodes
actions: Short-acting GTN for treatment and before planned exertion; repeat after 5 minutes; call an ambulance if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose (CG126).

clinicalManagement.title: Anti-anginal drugs
actions: First line: a beta-blocker or a calcium-channel blocker, chosen by comorbidities and preference; titrate to maximum tolerated dose.
Not controlled: switch to the other or combine — with a beta-blocker use a dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine, slow-release nifedipine, felodipine).
Beta-blocker and CCB both unsuitable: long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine as monotherapy or add-on.
Third drug only if uncontrolled on two and awaiting or unsuitable for revascularisation.

Atorvastatin 80 mg (NG238); target LDL 2.0 or non-HDL 2.6 mmol/L or less.

No vitamin or fish-oil supplements for angina (CG126).

pathophysiology.summary: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is acute coronary syndrome without persistent ST elevation in which a typical rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers shows myocardial injury. If the same symptoms occur without a biomarker rise, the label is unstable angina. The task is early risk stratification to choose between immediate, early, delayed or conservative management.
keyMechanisms: Partial or near-complete occlusion of a coronary artery reduces blood flow to the myocardium and causes myocardial injury (SHA printed pp. 22–23).
Typical ischaemic chest symptoms with a typical rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers are labelled NSTEMI; the same symptoms without a biomarker rise are labelled unstable angina (SHA printed p. 23).
Quantitative risk scoring predicts outcome better than clinical assessment alone in NSTE-ACS; the GRACE score gives the most accurate risk estimate on admission and at discharge (SHA printed p. 23).

Risk of future adverse events is categorised by predicted 6-month mortality: 1.5% or below lowest; over 1.5% to 3.0% low; over 3.0% to 6.0% intermediate; over 6.0% to 9.0% high; over 9.0% highest (NICE NG185 Table 1, Rec. 1.2.11).
Younger people with a low predicted mortality can still be at high risk of adverse cardiovascular events and may benefit from early angiography (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.15).

symptoms: Chest pressure or discomfort lasting at least several minutes, sometimes with sweating, dyspnoea, nausea or anxiety (SHA printed p. 23).

Score with the two-level PE Wells score; more than 4 points means PE likely (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.17). Troponin can also be raised in PE (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
Can raise troponin; consider it and use early CT to exclude it when troponin is raised (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.6.2 and 1.2.6.7). The cited sources do not list distinguishing symptoms.
Raised troponin without ACS; reassess for other causes before confirming ACS when troponin is raised (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
Constricting pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes; no troponin rise (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Initial treatment and monitoring
actions: Offer aspirin as soon as possible: a single loading dose of 300 mg unless clear allergy (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.2); the Saudi Heart Association gives 150–300 mg in aspirin-naive patients (SHA printed p. 25). Continue indefinitely unless bleeding risk or hypersensitivity contraindicates (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.1).
Do not give dual antiplatelet therapy before a diagnosis of unstable angina or NSTEMI is made (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.6).

Admit to a monitored unit. Continuous rhythm monitoring for at least 24 hours until NSTE-ACS is established or ruled out, and for those at intermediate or high risk of arrhythmia (SHA printed pp. 26–27).
Obtain troponin, creatinine, glucose, haemoglobin and lipid profile (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.8; SHA printed p. 26).

clinicalManagement.title: Choose the antithrombin
actions: Fondaparinux is recommended for people without high bleeding risk unless they are having immediate coronary angiography (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.3). SHA: fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously daily has the most favourable efficacy–safety profile (SHA printed p. 25).
Use unfractionated heparin rather than fondaparinux (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.3 and note).
Consider unfractionated heparin with dose adjusted to clotting monitoring (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.4).

branches.condition: High bleeding risk (age, known bleeding, renal impairment, low body weight)
actions: Choose the antithrombin and its dose carefully (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.5).
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily or unfractionated heparin (SHA printed p. 25). Do not cross over between unfractionated heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin (SHA printed p. 25).

clinicalManagement.title: Formal risk assessment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as the diagnosis and aspirin and antithrombin therapy are done
actions: Assess risk with an established score predicting 6-month mortality such as GRACE (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.7; SHA printed p. 23).
Include a full clinical history, examination with blood pressure and heart rate, a resting 12-lead ECG and blood tests (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.8).
Record the result in the care record and use it to balance treatment benefit against risk (NICE NG185 Recs 1.2.9–1.2.10).

clinicalManagement.title: Timing of coronary angiography
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediate, 24 hours, 72 hours or conservative, by risk group
actions: Pick the timing from the risk group. NICE and the Saudi Heart Association give different cut-offs; both are in the comparison table.

branches.condition: Clinically unstable, or very high-risk features
actions: NICE: offer immediate angiography (Rec. 1.2.12). SHA: immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours of admission (printed p. 24).

branches.condition: High risk (GRACE above 140, dynamic ST/T change, or troponin rise and/or fall compatible with MI)
actions: SHA: early invasive strategy within 24 hours of admission (printed p. 24). NICE: consider angiography within 72 hours if predicted 6-month mortality is above 3.0% (Rec. 1.2.13).

branches.condition: Intermediate risk (recurrent symptoms or substantial inducible ischaemia)
actions: SHA: invasive strategy within 72 hours (printed p. 24). NICE: consider angiography within 72 hours if predicted 6-month mortality is above 3.0% (Rec. 1.2.13).

branches.condition: Low risk (predicted 6-month mortality 3.0% or less; no recurrent symptoms)
actions: NICE: consider conservative management; consider angiography if ischaemia occurs or is shown on testing (Recs 1.2.14 and 1.2.20). SHA: non-invasive ischaemia testing, preferably with imaging, before deciding on invasive evaluation (printed pp. 24–25).
Some younger people with a low score may still be at high risk and benefit from early angiography (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.15).

clinicalManagement.title: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy around angiography and PCI
actions: Give unfractionated heparin systemically in the catheter laboratory to people having PCI, whether or not they received fondaparinux (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.16). SHA: single IV bolus of unfractionated heparin 70–85 IU/kg (50–60 IU/kg with concomitant GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors) in patients on fondaparinux (SHA printed p. 25).

Add a second antiplatelet to aspirin: prasugrel or ticagrelor if there is no separate indication for oral anticoagulation; clopidogrel if there is one. Give prasugrel only once coronary anatomy is defined and PCI is intended; think about bleeding risk at age 75 and over (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.17). SHA: ticagrelor, or clopidogrel if ticagrelor is unavailable, before or at the latest at PCI, for 12 months (printed p. 25).
If a stent is needed, use a drug-eluting stent (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.18). Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are an option as an adjunct to complex PCI (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.19).

Radial access is preferred in experienced centres (SHA printed p. 24). For multivessel disease, choose PCI or CABG with the Heart Team using clinical status, comorbidity and anatomy (SHA printed p. 24; NICE NG185 Recs 1.2.24–1.2.25).

clinicalManagement.title: When PCI is not indicated
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After angiography or with conservative management
actions: Offer ticagrelor with aspirin unless high bleeding risk (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.21). Consider clopidogrel with aspirin, or aspirin alone, if bleeding risk is high (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.22).
Consider ischaemia testing before discharge in people managed conservatively without angiography (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.26).
Before CABG, continue low-dose aspirin; in stabilised patients on DAPT consider stopping ticagrelor and clopidogrel 5 days before surgery (SHA printed p. 25).

clinicalManagement.title: Secondary prevention and before discharge
actions: Offer an ACE inhibitor as soon as haemodynamically stable, titrated up every 12 to 24 hours before discharge to the maximum tolerated or target dose; an ARB if intolerant; not both together (NICE NG185 Recs 1.4.6–1.4.9).

Offer a beta-blocker as soon as possible when haemodynamically stable (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.27). Avoid intravenous beta-blockers with hypotension, acute heart failure, AV block or severe bradycardia (SHA printed p. 26).
Start a high-dose statin as early as possible, with an LDL-C goal below 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) or a reduction of at least 50% (SHA printed p. 26).
Continue dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months after MI unless contraindicated (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.15). Assess bleeding risk at follow-up (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.3).
Keep blood glucose below 11.0 mmol/L while avoiding hypoglycaemia (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.3.1). Test HbA1c before discharge in people with hyperglycaemia without known diabetes (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.3.3).

Assess left ventricular function in everyone who has had NSTEMI (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.27). For symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, start an aldosterone antagonist within 3 to 14 days of MI, preferably after the ACE inhibitor (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.38).
Offer cardiac rehabilitation with an exercise component to everyone, starting within 10 days of discharge (NICE NG185 Recs 1.8.1 and 1.8.13).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus ischaemic symptoms, new ST-T change or new LBBB, pathological Q waves, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or wall motion abnormality, or intracoronary thrombus at angiography

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: NSTEMI versus unstable angina (SHA printed p. 23)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Typical ischaemic symptoms with a typical rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers = NSTEMI; same symptoms without a biomarker rise = unstable angina

Ongoing ischaemia, haemodynamic compromise, arrhythmia, mechanical complication of MI, acute heart failure, or recurrent dynamic or widespread ST/T changes: immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours of admission
GRACE score above 140, dynamic ST and/or T-wave changes, or a troponin rise and/or fall compatible with MI: early invasive strategy within 24 hours of admission
Recurrent symptoms or substantial inducible ischaemia on provocative testing: invasive strategy within 72 hours of admission
Clinically unstable: offer immediate coronary angiography

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Intermediate or higher risk (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.13)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Predicted 6-month mortality above 3.0% with no contraindication: consider coronary angiography within 72 hours of first admission
Predicted 6-month mortality 3.0% or less: consider conservative management; consider angiography if ischaemia later occurs or is shown on testing

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Score 2 to 306. Risk of all-cause mortality by 6 months as printed: 60–100 about 3%; 100–140 about 8%; 140–180 about 20%; above 180 above 40% (ranges overlap at 100, 140 and 180 as printed)

learningObjectives: Distinguish NSTEMI from unstable angina and from STEMI using ECG and troponin.
Risk-stratify with GRACE and choose the timing of angiography.
Select antiplatelet and antithrombin therapy and plan secondary prevention.
pitfalls: Starting dual antiplatelet therapy before the diagnosis of NSTEMI is made (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.6).
Giving prasugrel before coronary anatomy is defined (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.17) or to patients with prior stroke or TIA (FDA label).
Crossing over between unfractionated and low-molecular-weight heparin (SHA printed p. 25).
Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB after MI without another reason (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.8).
Treating a troponin rise as ACS without considering myocarditis, aortic dissection or PE (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
keyPoints: NSTEMI = typical symptoms plus a typical rise and fall of biomarkers; unstable angina has no rise (SHA).
Aspirin early; do not start dual antiplatelet therapy before the diagnosis is made (NICE).
Angiography timing is by risk: immediate or within 2 hours if unstable or very high risk; within 24 hours (SHA high risk); within 72 hours for intermediate risk.
Fondaparinux is first choice unless immediate angiography, high bleeding risk or creatinine above 265 micromol/L.

patientEducation: Offer clear information on the risks and benefits of each treatment, matched to the person's underlying risk and comorbidities, so they can choose a management strategy (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.23).

Explain that sexual activity after recovery carries no greater risk of triggering another MI; most people with an uncomplicated recovery can resume after about 4 weeks when comfortable (NICE NG185 Recs 1.8.32–1.8.33).
Give a copy of the discharge summary to the person (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.7.2).
Advise people without known diabetes who had hyperglycaemia that they are at increased risk of type 2 diabetes and should be tested at least annually (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.3.6).
lifestyleAndDiet: Mediterranean-style diet; do not advise omega-3 capsules or beta-carotene supplements to prevent another MI (NICE NG185 Recs 1.9.1, 1.9.3 and 1.9.5).
Physical activity for 20 to 30 minutes a day to the point of slight breathlessness, built up gradually (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.9.11).
Identify smokers and give repeated advice with follow-up support, nicotine replacement, varenicline or bupropion (SHA printed p. 27; NICE NG185 Recs 1.9.13–1.9.14).
Support to achieve and maintain a healthy weight if overweight or obese (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.9.15).
mdtReferrals: Cardiology and interventional cardiology; Heart Team (interventional cardiologist, cardiac surgeon and others) when the revascularisation strategy is unclear (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.25; SHA printed p. 24).
Cardiac rehabilitation or structured secondary prevention for all patients hospitalised with NSTE-ACS (SHA printed p. 27; NICE NG185 Rec. 1.8.1).
Cardiological assessment for revascularisation in anyone with previous MI who has not had it (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.5.1).
dischargeCriteria: Diagnosis confirmed, risk assessed and revascularisation decision made, with antiplatelet, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and statin started (NICE NG185 Recs 1.2.7, 1.4.1 and 1.5.1).
Left ventricular function assessed and recorded (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.27 and 1.2.29).
Discharge summary includes confirmation of acute MI, results of investigations, incomplete drug titrations, future management plans and secondary prevention advice (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.7.1).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Send the GP a clear management plan with further drug titration, blood pressure and renal function monitoring (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.2). Re-check lipids 4–6 weeks after the event (SHA printed p. 26). Reassess at 3 months and then at least annually (SHA printed p. 27). If pre-discharge LVEF is 40% or below, repeat echocardiography 6–12 weeks after MI (SHA printed p. 27). Begin cardiac rehabilitation within 10 days of discharge (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.8.13).
